body.text: With barely a month remaining before the 30-year India–Bangladesh Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires, there is little public evidence of a serious political push towards its renewal. Although technical-level discussions have continued under the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC), the larger question remains whether the two governments are building on these engagements towards a renewed agreement.

The 1996 treaty had reset the tone, establishing a framework for moving beyond historical mistrust. Its renewal could offer an opportunity to demonstrate that bilateral cooperation is not contingent on political partnership between governments. Conversely, its failure would risk turning a longstanding water-sharing concern into another symbol of the deterioration in relations. Although the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina from New Delhi currently occupies much of Dhaka’s attention, the sensitive issue of water-sharing remains a priority for Bangladesh.

The most pressing concern is not that the two countries may fail to arrive at a new agreement before the deadline but that the absence of a political breakthrough could further strain the fragile relationship. Bangladesh is seeking revised guarantees over its share of water, while India is concentrating on the existing institutional mechanism of the Joint Rivers Commission. Their differences are not merely procedural; they go to the substance and assurances of the future arrangement.
If the Ganges agreement is allowed to lapse, what signal would it send about the capacity of the two countries to manage other shared concerns?

Since August 2024, India and Bangladesh have largely managed their relationship through limited engagement. The political rupture following Sheikh Hasina's departure for India and the subsequent transformation of Bangladesh's domestic political landscape fundamentally altered the relationship. There have been some efforts to restore consular and educational services and maintain essential diplomatic communication. However, much of the wider architecture of bilateral cooperation remains impaired. Cross-border connectivity, transit arrangements, trade facilitation and other institutional mechanisms that had taken years to develop have either been restricted or lost momentum. The change in Dhaka inevitably required India to recalibrate its approach. It also created expectations in Bangladesh that the relationship would be reset on a different political footing.

Following the February 2026 elections, and Tarique Rahman's assumption of office, there appeared to be an opportunity for such a reset. However, a proposed state visit to India remains elusive, mired in roadblocks and Dhaka's insistence on a conducive political environment, including the extradition of Sheikh Hasina and those accused of killing Hadi, a Bangladeshi rising political star. These concerns, and Sheikh Hasina’s intention to return to Bangladesh by the end of the year, have added to unease in Dhaka.

Under the existing treaty, Bangladesh is allocated a share during the annual dry season (January–May), determined by a formula based on available river flows and a 10-day periodic system of water distribution. But the lack of a minimum guarantee clause has been a preoccupation in Bangladesh. The expiry of the treaty would not automatically mean that India could stop releasing water to Bangladesh, or that Bangladesh would immediately lose access to the Ganges. However, it would remove the agreed bilateral framework that currently governs the sharing of dry-season flows at Farakka, a barrage vital to the system.
Ganges water-sharing cannot be treated as a technical issue, particularly when the livelihoods of populations on both sides of the border are increasingly at risk (Rudra Gupta/Unsplash).

Ganges water-sharing cannot be treated as a technical issue, particularly when climate variability, changing river flows, dry-season scarcity, sedimentation and the livelihoods of populations on both sides of the border are increasingly at risk. A renewed agreement would need to address contemporary hydrological realities rather than simply reproduce the assumptions and arrangements of 1996. Bangladesh's demand for greater assurances and India's need to accommodate the concerns of its riparian states, particularly West Bengal and Bihar, will require sustained political negotiation and accommodation.

The lack of active bilateral relations between the neighbours is especially problematic, and the absence of visible confrontation should not be mistaken for the existence of stability. India and Bangladesh share 54 transboundary rivers, an extensive land border, interconnected economies and significant security and connectivity interests. Their geographical realities make prolonged diplomatic disengagement difficult to sustain.

If the Ganges agreement is allowed to lapse, what signal would it send about the capacity of the two countries to manage other shared concerns? There appears to be no agreement over the long-standing Teesta River dispute, border management continues to generate friction, and trade and transit arrangements have become entangled in broader political issues. The lack of a Ganges treaty could reinforce the perception that even established bilateral mechanisms are vulnerable to political disagreements.

Ultimately, the question confronting New Delhi and Dhaka is not whether they can return to the relationship that existed before August 2024, but whether the two neighbours are able to accommodate their differences while preserving the institutional and economic foundations of cooperation. Once again, the common people will be paying for the consequences of politics.
Prof Sreeradha Datta teaches International Affairs at O.P. Jindal Global University (Haryana, India) and is a non-resident Senior Fellow at ISAS, National University of Singapore.
